seasons.label: When to go
seasons.heading: Seasonal visiting strategy
seasons.intro: Three seasons shape life in the old city, plus one annual air-quality window that matters more than the thermometer. This table combines temperature, rainfall, haze and visitor density so you can choose your weeks.
seasons.climateNote: Temperature and rainfall figures follow the WMO 1991–2020 standard normals for the Chiang Mai station; the hazy period reflects the agricultural burning season typical of February–April across the northern provinces.

rows.advice: The best all-round window: warm days, cool evenings. Reserve accommodation early for December and January, and arrive before 09:00 for quiet photographs.
Visit early in the morning or wait for the first rains in late April. Travellers with respiratory sensitivity should check the daily air-quality index before walking far.
Plan the temple before 10:00 or after 16:00. Carry water, use the shaded courtyards, and expect the stone terraces to be hot underfoot at midday.

rows.air: Cleanest air of the year, quietest temple
rows.advice: Mornings are usually dry and the courtyards are almost empty. Expect heavy but short showers after 15:00 — the wet stone and low clouds make this the most photogenic season.

seasons.tip: Whatever the season, the temple grounds open early. The two hours after sunrise give you soft light, cool air and the fewest visitors.

routes.label: Plan by traveller
routes.heading: Three routes for three kinds of visitors
routes.intro: The compound is compact, so the difference between routes is pace and focus rather than distance. Choose the one that matches who you are travelling with.

audiences.title: Families with children
audiences.text: Enter from Ratchapakhinai Road and make the elephant-backed chedi the first stop — children usually find the stone elephants before they notice the gold. Then rest in the shaded courtyard and finish at the ordination-hall terrace.

audiences.title: Photography & architecture
audiences.text: Work clockwise from the viharn: the naga staircase balustrades, the teak ordination hall, the elephant chedi in raking light, then the scripture library. Late afternoon adds warm light on the goldwork.

audiences.title: Low-effort & step-free
audiences.text: The main approach from Ratchapakhinai Road is level. A single loop along the courtyard edge covers the chedi, the ordination hall exterior and the city pillar shrine without climbing steps; low kerbs remain in places.

itinerary.label: Suggested routes
itinerary.heading: Half-day and full-day plans
itinerary.intro: Both plans start at Wat Chiang Man and stay inside the old city walls, so everything is reachable on foot or with one short ride.

halfDay.title: Half day (about 3 hours)
halfDay.summary: The temple plus the two or three neighbouring monuments that give it context.

steps.title: Arrive at Wat Chiang Man
steps.text: Cool air, soft light and the monks' morning routine. Start at the elephant-backed chedi.

steps.title: Ordination hall & city pillar
steps.text: Step inside the main hall, then see the city pillar shrine that ties the temple to the founding of the city.

steps.title: Walk south to Wat Phra Singh
steps.text: A 15-minute walk through the old city to Chiang Mai's other great temple complex.

steps.title: Three Kings Monument
steps.text: The square in front of the former provincial hall, where the founding alliance of the city is commemorated.

fullDay.title: Full day (about 8 hours)
fullDay.summary: The temple, the old city, a museum stop and an evening market.

steps.title: Wat Chiang Man

facilities.label: Visitor services
facilities.heading: Facilities in and around the temple
facilities.intro: A short, practical overview of what exists within a few minutes of the gate — described by type only, so you know what to look for rather than which shop to visit.
facilities.neutralNote: As an independent non-profit guide we do not recommend individual businesses. Categories, distances and the usual price level are given instead; opening hours and prices change often, so confirm locally.

items.title: Restrooms
items.text: Public toilets are available inside the temple grounds near the entrance and car park. They are basic but maintained; carry your own tissues and hand sanitiser as a precaution.

items.title: Parking
items.text: A compact parking area inside the compound serves cars and scooters. It fills up around midday in high season; roadside parking along Ratchapakhinai Road is the usual fallback.

items.title: Food & drink
items.text: Within a five-minute walk you will find small family-run restaurants, coffee stands and a morning market selling northern Thai dishes. Vegetarian options are common in the old city.

items.title: Accommodation
items.text: The old city offers a full range, from budget guesthouses to small boutique hotels, mostly low-rise buildings in converted shophouses. Staying inside the moat puts the temple within walking distance.

items.title: Groceries & convenience
items.text: Convenience stores and small minimarkets line the main roads inside the moat, most open long hours. A traditional market near the moat sells fruit, drinking water and daily goods.

items.title: Fuel & EV charging
items.text: Fuel stations sit on the moat ring road about five minutes away by car, and public AC/DC charge points for electric vehicles are available at shopping centres and larger hotels on the ring roads.

items.title: Medical & pharmacy
items.text: Pharmacies are frequent in the old city and can handle minor complaints. For anything serious, general and private hospitals are roughly ten to fifteen minutes by car; keep travel insurance details handy.

items.title: Cash & banking
items.text: ATMs and licensed exchange kiosks are found along the main streets inside the moat. Small temples and market stalls are cash-only, so keep some banknotes for donations and snacks.

facilities.walkingNote: Distances from the temple gate: convenience store 2–4 min · restaurant 3–5 min · pharmacy 5–8 min · fuel station 5 min by car.

responsibility.label: Science & visitor responsibility
responsibility.heading: How to visit respectfully
responsibility.intro: Wat Chiang Man is a working monastery as well as a monument: roughly sixty monks and novices live and study here. Understanding what you are looking at makes the visit better, and a little care keeps it that way.

groups.title: Dress & entering
points: Cover shoulders and knees; a light scarf solves most problems in seconds.
Remove shoes before entering a hall, and never point the soles of your feet towards a Buddha image.
Take off hats inside buildings and step over — never on — the raised threshold.

groups.title: Conduct & quiet
points: Keep voices low; chanting and lessons take place most mornings and late afternoons.
Do not touch murals, Buddha images or the carved woodwork — skin oils damage them permanently.
Ask before photographing monks, and never photograph a person at prayer.

groups.title: Offerings & the environment
points: Entry is free; donations are voluntary and go to the monastery's upkeep.
Leave no litter, and prefer a refillable bottle — the old city has several refill points.
Drones and tripods are not appropriate inside a monastery without written permission.

responsibility.pledge: Take photographs, leave nothing behind, and let the people who worship here set the pace. That is the whole of temple etiquette.
responsibility.scienceNote: Why it matters: lime plaster murals, teak structures and sandstone reliefs in northern Thailand survive in a hot, humid climate only because they are looked after daily. Humidity, flash photography and touching are the three things that age them fastest.

legends.label: Stories & chronicles
legends.heading: Legends behind the temple
legends.intro: Northern Thai history is recorded in palm-leaf chronicles known as tamnan, where fact, faith and royal propaganda sit side by side. These are the stories that attach to Wat Chiang Man.

stories.title: The resting place of the white elephant
stories.text: King Mangrai is said to have chosen this ground while searching for a new capital: a white elephant — the ultimate symbol of royal authority in the region — stopped here, trumpeted three times and refused to move. The king built his camp, 'Wiang Chiang Man', around it, and the later city of Chiang Mai grew outward from that camp.

stories.title: Phra Sae Tang Khamani, the crystal Buddha
stories.text: A small image carved from clear crystal, it is said to have been brought from the Mon kingdom of Lavo (today's Lopburi) and carried north by Mangrai himself. Tradition credits it with protecting the city from storm and fire. It is normally kept in the raised scripture library and shown publicly during the Songkran festival in April.

stories.title: Phra Sila and the promise of rain
stories.text: A sandstone relief of the Buddha, Phra Sila is the temple's other great image. Because it is associated with rain-making, it is carried through the streets of the old city at Songkran so that townspeople can pour scented water over it and ask for a good growing season.

stories.title: The pact of the three kings
stories.text: Before founding Chiang Mai, Mangrai of Lanna, Ramkhamhaeng of Sukhothai and Ngam Mueang of Phayao are said to have sworn an alliance that secured the northern valleys. The Three Kings Monument, a short walk from the temple, commemorates it — and explains why this corner of the old city is treated as the city's birthplace.

stories.title: Nagas, elephants and guardian serpents
stories.text: The staircases of the viharns are flanked by balustrades in the form of nagas, the serpent water spirits of Buddhist cosmology, while the great chedi rests on rows of sculpted elephants. Together they state the temple's purpose in stone: the Buddha's teaching upheld by the power of the earth.

legends.note: Chronicle traditions, not documented fact. Where the chronicles and archaeology disagree, the inscriptions and excavation reports are the better guide — but the stories are what local people have told for seven centuries.

about.label: About
about.heading: Chiang Mai’s first temple
about.headingEntity: About Wat Chiang Man — Chiang Mai’s First Temple
about.entityLead: Welcome to **Wat Chiang Man** (วัดเชียงมั่น), the temple that **watchiangman.com** is dedicated to. Located in the heart of **Chiang Mai**, **Chiang Mai** Province, **Thailand**, it is the oldest temple inside the old city walls and a primary landmark for travellers visiting the region.
about.lead: Tucked into the quiet north of the old walled city, Wat Chiang Man is where Chiang Mai began — both as a sacred site and as a royal residence.
about.paragraph1: In 1296 King Mangrai (Mengrai) chose this spot as his base while laying out the new Lanna capital. He built a modest pavilion here and lived in it during the city’s founding — making Wat Chiang Man the oldest temple within Chiang Mai’s moat.
about.paragraph2: Centuries later the temple remains a living place of worship. Its whitewashed walls, weathered teak and small scale give it an intimacy the larger city temples lack, even as it guards two of northern Thailand’s most revered Buddha images.
about.quote: “To stand in Wat Chiang Man is to stand where Chiang Mai itself was born.”

etymology.title: What “Chiang Man” means
etymology.text: In Lanna / Thai, “Chiang” (เชียง) means “city”, and “Man” (มั่น) means “firm, enduring”. So “Chiang Man” reads as “the stable city” — King Mangrai’s wish that his new capital would endure.

highlights.title: Phra Sae Tang Khamani
highlights.desc: An 11th-century crystal Buddha believed to protect the city and bring rain.

highlights.title: Phra Sila
highlights.desc: A revered stone image linked to Sri Lanka and the rainy season.

highlights.title: Chiang Man stupas
highlights.desc: Two square stupas resting on the backs of ornate elephants.

editorTip.text: Dress modestly, remove your shoes in the halls, and aim for an early morning visit to enjoy the temple in peace.

arch.label: Architecture & Treasures
arch.heading: Sacred art of the Lanna court
arch.intro: Wat Chiang Man is a compact museum of Lanna craft — from its square elephant-backed stupas to the two small Buddhas that have drawn pilgrims for nearly a thousand years.

treasures.title: The crystal Buddha
treasures.text: Carved from a single crystal and dated to the 11th century, this small standing Buddha is also called Phra Kaew Khao ('the white jewel'). It is paraded through the old city during Songkran to invite rain and fortune.

treasures.title: The stone Buddha
treasures.text: A sandstone relief image associated with Sri Lanka, long credited with rain-making powers. Devotees still venerate it for protection and a good harvest.

architecture.title: Elephant-backed chedis
architecture.desc: Two cubical stupas (13th c.) sit on tiers of stucco elephants — the iconic 'Chiang Man' form unique to this temple, formally named Chedi Chang Lom (เจดีย์ช้างล้อม, 'stupa surrounded by elephants').

architecture.title: Viharn Luang
architecture.desc: The main hall, rebuilt in the 1920s on the original foundations; its old teak pillars are preserved inside.

architecture.title: Ubosot (ordination hall)
architecture.desc: A smaller, quieter hall used for monastic rites, with fine Lanna woodwork.

arch.noteText: The two treasures are kept in the small library-style structure (ho trai) on the right; ask a monk if you’d like a closer look.

history.label: History
history.heading: From royal camp to city shrine
history.headingEntity: History & Significance of Wat Chiang Man
history.compareBefore: Wat Chiang Man main viharn facade
history.compareAfter: Elephant-backed chedi at Wat Chiang Man
history.compareHint: Drag the slider left and right to compare architectural details
history.intro: Wat Chiang Man’s story is the story of Chiang Mai’s founding — a temple that began as a king’s temporary dwelling and grew into the city’s spiritual heart.

blocks.title: Mangrai’s encampment
blocks.text: King Mangrai of the Lanna kingdom chose the site as his headquarters while founding Chiang Mai, living in a pavilion that became the temple’s nucleus.

blocks.title: The elephant chedis
blocks.text: The two square stupas on elephant backs were raised, establishing the distinctive Chiang Man architectural style.

blocks.title: Rebuilding the viharn
blocks.text: The main assembly hall was reconstructed on its original footprint, preserving the ancient teak columns within.

blocks.title: A living temple
blocks.text: Wat Chiang Man remains an active monastery and the most visited of Chiang Mai’s historic temples.

legend.title: The rain-making Buddhas
legend.text: Both Phra Sae Tang Khamani and Phra Sila are believed to control the rains. In times of drought, the crystal Buddha was once carried in procession to summon the monsoon.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Wat Chiang Man sits inside the square moat of the old city’s northwest quarter — the exact area where Mangrai first laid out his capital.

folklore.title: The crystal that calls the rain
folklore.tale: Local lore says the white crystal Buddha 'speaks' through the weather: when it is taken out for Songkran, the skies open and the rice fields drink. Farmers still watch its procession as a blessing for the year ahead.
folklore.shrine: The crystal Buddha rests in the ho trai (scripture library) on the temple’s right side, brought out for public viewing during Songkran each April.

guide.label: Visitor Guide
guide.heading: Plan a calm, respectful visit
guide.lead: Wat Chiang Man is free to enter and easy to reach on foot from anywhere in the old city. A little planning makes the experience far richer.

items.title: Temple entry
items.desc: Free. A small donation at the booth supports upkeep and the monks.

items.title: Dress code
items.desc: Shoulders and knees covered; remove shoes in all halls.

items.title: Photography
items.desc: Allowed in the grounds; avoid flash and never photograph monks without asking.

items.title: From the airport
items.desc: Chiang Mai International Airport (CNX) is ~5 km from the Old City. Specific steps:
steps: Arrive at the domestic or international arrival hall.
Book an official airport taxi near Exit 1 or use the Grab/Bolt app (approx. 150–200 THB).
Ask the driver to go to 'Wat Chiang Man' inside the Old City.
The driver will drop you off right at the main entrance on Ratchapakhinai Road.

items.title: On foot
items.desc: 10–15 min walk from Tha Phae Gate or most old-city guesthouses.

items.title: Songthaew / red truck
items.desc: Hop a red songthaew and ask for 'Wat Chiang Man' near Ratchapakhinai Rd.

items.title: Tuk-tuk / Grab
items.desc: A short, inexpensive ride from anywhere in the city centre.

accessibility.intro: The temple grounds are flat and mostly step-free; the halls have a few thresholds.

guide.faqTitle: Wat Chiang Man FAQ — entry fee, hours, dress code & history

faqs.q: Where is Wat Chiang Man located?
faqs.a: Wat Chiang Man is located at 171 Ratchapakhinai Rd, Old City, Si Phum, Mueang Chiang Mai District, Chiang Mai 50200, Thailand (18.7938, 98.9867), inside the old city moat.

faqs.q: Is Wat Chiang Man free to visit?
faqs.a: Yes. Wat Chiang Man is a public temple and is free to visit year-round; donations are welcome but never required.

faqs.q: How old is Wat Chiang Man?
faqs.a: It was founded in 1296 by King Mangrai, making it the oldest temple in Chiang Mai.
Yes. Donations are welcome but not required.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Wat Chiang Man?
faqs.a: The temple grounds are open daily from about 05:00 to 19:00; there is no closing day.

faqs.q: Can I see the crystal Buddha?
faqs.a: It is kept in the ho trai and shown publicly during Songkran (April); at other times, ask a monk.
30–60 minutes is enough to see the highlights at a relaxed pace.

faqs.q: What is the dress code at Wat Chiang Man?
faqs.a: Cover shoulders and knees, and remove your shoes before stepping into any hall. A light scarf or sarong solves most outfit problems on the spot.

faqs.q: Is Wat Chiang Man the oldest temple in Chiang Mai?
faqs.a: Yes. It was founded in 1296 by King Mangrai while he was laying out the new Lanna capital, which makes it the oldest temple inside the old city moat.

faqs.q: How do I get to Wat Chiang Man from Tha Phae Gate?
faqs.a: It is a 15-20 minute walk north through the old city, or a short red songthaew ride — ask for Ratchapakhinai Road. The temple is on the corner near the city pillar shrine.

footer.about: An independent visitor guide to Wat Chiang Man (วัดเชียงมั่น) — Chiang Mai’s first temple, founded by King Mangrai in 1296.
footer.note: Free entry, daily 05:00–19:00. Dress modestly and remove shoes in the halls.

etiquette.label: Temple etiquette
etiquette.heading: How to visit respectfully
etiquette.lead: Wat Chiang Man is a working monastery — around a hundred monks and novices live and study here. These few habits keep the visit comfortable for everyone.

columns.title: Dress code
items: Cover shoulders and knees — no singlets or shorts inside the halls
Shoes off before stepping onto any raised hall platform
Sarongs are rented near the gate for about 100 THB

columns.title: Conduct
items: Greet with a wai, palms together at the chest
Never point the soles of your feet at a Buddha image

columns.title: Worship sequence
items: Light the candle and incense, then kneel or stand with palms together
Offer the lotus, then press a leaf of gold onto the image
Sprinkle a little lustral water and bow three times

chant.title: What the chant means
chant.meaning: “Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One” — recited three times to open a ceremony. It honours the Buddha rather than asking for anything.
chant.note: You will hear Sadhu (สาธุ) at the end of a blessing: “so be it”. Repeating it back is the simplest way to join in.
